claim: In vivo, wide-field GCaMP imaging and sub-cortical/cortical cellular electrophysiology were used in mice to investigate relationships between spontaneous single neuron spiking and mesoscopic cortical activity.
source: In vivo, wide-field GCaMP imaging and sub-cortical/cortical cellular electrophysiology were used in mice to investigate relationships between spontaneous single neuron spiking and mesoscopic cortical activity.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: A mesoscale spike-triggered averaging procedure allowed the identification of motifs that are preferentially linked to individual spiking neurons by employing genetically targeted indicators of neuronal activity.
source: A mesoscale spike-triggered averaging procedure allowed the identification of motifs that are preferentially linked to individual spiking neurons by employing genetically targeted indicators of neuronal activity.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach and its capability.

claim: Thalamic neurons predicted and reported specific cycles of wide-scale cortical inhibition/excitation.
source: Thalamic neurons predicted and reported specific cycles of wide-scale cortical inhibition/excitation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Spike-triggered maps derived from single cortical neurons yielded spatio-temporal maps expected for regional cortical consensus function.
source: In contrast, spike-triggered maps derived from single cortical neurons yielded spatio-temporal maps expected for regional cortical consensus function.
evidence: This is a primary finding contrasting cortical and thalamic neuron behavior.

claim: Mesoscale networks occupy an intermediate space and are well studied in cortex forming the basis of sensory and motor maps.
source: Mesoscale networks occupy an intermediate space and are well studied in cortex forming the basis of sensory and motor maps (Bohland et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The study of large-scale networks (meso-to macroscale) has been mostly restricted to functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), or magnetoencephalography that can capture whole-brain activity patterns but lack high spatial and temporal resolution and sensitivity.
source: The study of large-scale networks (meso-to macroscale) has been mostly restricted to functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), or magnetoencephalography that can capture whole-brain activity patterns (de Pasquale et al., 2010; Kahn et al., 2011; Logothetis et al., 2012), but lack high spatial and temporal resolution and sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing limitations of existing methods.

claim: Alternative approaches including mesoscopic intrinsic signal, voltage, glutamate, or calcium sensitive indicator imaging have been employed to overcome limitations of fMRI and magnetoencephalography.
source: To overcome these limitations, alternative approaches including mesoscopic intrinsic signal, voltage, glutamate, or calcium sensitive indicator imaging have been employed (Kleinfeld et al., 1994; Kenet et al., 2003; Ferezou et al., 2007; Chemla and Chavane, 2010; Chen et al., 2013b; Mohajerani et al., 2013; Stroh et al., 2013; Vanni and Murphy, 2014; Carandini et al., 2015; Chan et al., 2015; Madisen et al., 2015; Wekselblatt et al., 2016; Xie et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to previous work.

claim: GCaMP imaging offers a high signal-to-noise ratio and is associated with supra-threshold activity which allows a more direct comparison with spike activity.
source: While slower than protein-based or small molecule voltage sensors, GCaMP imaging offers a high signal-to-noise ratio and is associated with supra-threshold activity which allows a more direct comparison with spike activity.
evidence: This describes a property of the GCaMP indicator used in the study.

claim: Spike-triggered averaging (STA) was used to identify the local activity profile related to the spiking activity of a single neuron within a population.
source: Spike-triggered averaging (STA) was used to identify the local activity profile related to the spiking activity of a single neuron within this population (Arieli et al., 1995)
evidence: This describes a methodological approach with citation to pioneering work.

claim: The activity profile could reveal the instantaneous spatial pattern of ongoing population activity related to a neuron's optimal stimulus in visual cortex of anesthetized cat.
source: it was further demonstrated that this activity profile could reveal the instantaneous spatial pattern of ongoing population activity related to a neuron's optimal stimulus in visual cortex of anesthetized cat (Tsodyks et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Spontaneous activity in awake and anesthetized mice was exploited as a source of diverse cortical network activity motifs.
source: Spontaneous activity in awake and anesthetized mice was exploited as a source of diverse cortical network activity motifs (Mohajerani et al., 2010, 2013; Chan et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach with supporting citations.

claim: Single thalamic neuron spikes were found to functionally link to multiple primary sensorimotor maps.
source: Single thalamic neuron spikes were found to functionally link to multiple primary sensorimotor maps
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Spiking cortical neurons were largely associated with consensus cortical maps.
source: in contrast spiking cortical neurons were largely associated with consensus cortical maps.
evidence: This is a primary finding contrasting with thalamic neurons.

claim: Thalamic neurons were found to both predict and report (firing before and after) specific cycles of wide-scale cortical inhibition/excitation.
source: Thalamic neurons were found to both predict and report (firing before and after) specific cycles of wide-scale cortical inhibition/excitation
evidence: This is a primary finding describing temporal relationships.

claim: Cortical neuron firing was usually associated with excitation.
source: while cortical neuron firing was usually associated with excitation.
evidence: This is a primary finding contrasting cortical and thalamic behavior.

claim: These results are consistent with an active computational role of thalamus in sensory-motor processing as opposed to merely serving a relay function.
source: These results are consistent with an active computational role of thalamus in sensory-motor processing (Theyel et al., 2010; Hooks et al., 2013; Petrus et al., 2014; Sheroziya and Timofeev, 2014; McCormick et al., 2015), as opposed to merely serving a relay function
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations to related work.

claim: The results are consistent with a diverse role of the thalamus in feedforward sensory processing.
source: and is consistent with a diverse role of the thalamus in feedforward sensory processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Thalamocortical transmission can dynamically and differentially recruit local cortical excitation and inhibition based on thalamic neuron firing patterns.
source: Thalamocortical transmission can dynamically and differentially recruit local cortical excitation and inhibition based on thalamic neuron firing patterns and where thalamocortical feedforward inhibition is a critical feature (Galarreta and Hestrin, 1998; Swadlow and Gusev, 2001; Gabernet et al., 2005; Cruikshank et al., 2007; Hu and Agmon, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Thalamocortical feedforward inhibition is a critical feature of thalamocortical transmission.
source: Thalamocortical transmission can dynamically and differentially recruit local cortical excitation and inhibition based on thalamic neuron firing patterns and where thalamocortical feedforward inhibition is a critical feature (Galarreta and Hestrin, 1998; Swadlow and Gusev, 2001; Gabernet et al., 2005; Cruikshank et al., 2007; Hu and Agmon, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: This spike-triggered cortical mapping technique can be extended to any brain location where electrodes can be placed to identify functionally linked cortical mesoscale networks.
source: We expect that this spike-triggered cortical mapping technique, exploiting mesoscopic calcium imaging, can be extended to any brain location where electrodes can be placed to identify functionally linked cortical mesoscale networks.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications.

claim: Cortical and sub-cortical neuron spiking activities were recorded electrically while simultaneously imaging cortical mesoscopic activity across a 9 × 9 mm bilateral window.
source: Cortical and sub-cortical neuron spiking activities were recorded electrically while simultaneously imaging cortical mesoscopic activity across a 9 × 9 mm bilateral window that encompassed multiple areas of the mouse dorsal cortex including somatosensory, motor, visual, retrosplenial, parietal association and cingulate areas (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup with reference to figures.

claim: The imaging window encompassed multiple areas of the mouse dorsal cortex including somatosensory, motor, visual, retrosplenial, parietal association and cingulate areas.
source: Cortical and sub-cortical neuron spiking activities were recorded electrically while simultaneously imaging cortical mesoscopic activity across a 9 × 9 mm bilateral window that encompassed multiple areas of the mouse dorsal cortex including somatosensory, motor, visual, retrosplenial, parietal association and cingulate areas (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This describes the spatial coverage of the imaging.

claim: Spectral decomposition of the mesoscopic spontaneous activity using GCaMP6 revealed the presence of information below 10 Hz that was distinct from non-specific green light reflectance.
source: Spectral decomposition of the mesoscopic spontaneous activity using GCaMP6 revealed the presence of information below 10 Hz that was distinct from non-specific green light reflectance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Deconvolution improved the temporal dynamics of the decay of the calcium signal.
source: While deconvolution improved the temporal dynamics of the decay of the calcium signal, spike-triggered analysis was only marginally affected and it was not used throughout.
evidence: This describes the effect of a data processing method.

claim: Spike-triggered analysis was only marginally affected by deconvolution.
source: While deconvolution improved the temporal dynamics of the decay of the calcium signal, spike-triggered analysis was only marginally affected and it was not used throughout.
evidence: This describes the limited impact of deconvolution on the main analysis.

claim: Spiking signals were initially recorded in multiple brain areas using glass electrodes to minimize obstruction of cortical imaging and reduce potential for damage from electrode placement.
source: Spiking signals were initially recorded in multiple brain areas using glass electrodes (n = 8 mice) to minimize obstruction of cortical imaging and reduce potential for damage from electrode placement.
evidence: This describes the methodological choice and rationale.

claim: Laminar probes permitted the resolution of more spiking neurons simultaneously and facilitated the recordings in multiple sub-cortical regions.
source: Subsequently, laminar probes (16 channel with 0.1 mm contact spacing) permitted the resolution of more spiking neurons simultaneously, and facilitated the recordings in multiple sub-cortical regions (n = 16 mice).
evidence: This describes the advantages of using laminar probes.

claim: Initial data were obtained from urethane or isoflurane anesthetized adult mice.
source: Given the invasive nature and the long duration of recordings, initial data were obtained from urethane (n = 4) or isoflurane (n = 12) anesthetized adult mice, but were later optimized to include awake recordings (n = 12, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: The spike-triggered average maps (STMs) obtained under anesthetized and awake conditions were qualitatively similar.
source: The spike-triggered average maps (STMs) obtained under both these conditions were qualitatively similar, and this observation was consistent with previous work using VSD imaging (Mohajerani et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding comparing different experimental conditions, supported by citation.

claim: Single neuron spikes were identified from extracellular recordings using spike sorting methods based on clustering of principal components distributions of spike signals on sets of adjacent channels.
source: To perform these assessments, we identified single neuron spikes from extracellular recordings using spike sorting methods based on clustering of principal components distributions of spike signals on sets of adjacent channels (Swindale and Spacek, 2014) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the spike sorting methodology with citation.

claim: The static STM was defined as the peak response calculated for each pixel within a time window of ±1 s.
source: The static STM was then defined as the peak response (in units of ΔF/F0) calculated for each pixel within a time window of ±1 s.
evidence: This defines a key methodological parameter.

claim: The peak method is a better reflection of correlated activity than the average over the ±1 s interval which would smooth out highly activated – but short duration activity increases.
source: This peak method is a better reflection of correlated activity than the average over the ±1 s interval which would smooth out highly activated – but short duration activity increases.
evidence: This provides rationale for the methodological choice.

claim: The activity recorded from a single right barrel cortex neuron yielded an STM showing strong and specific GCaMP signal in the barrel and motor cortices of both hemispheres.
source: This method revealed that the activity recorded from a single right barrel cortex neuron yielded an STM showing strong and specific GCaMP signal in the barrel and motor cortices of both hemispheres (Figure 1Ei).
evidence: This is an example result shown in a figure.

claim: Imaging Thy-1 GFP-M mice that lacked calcium-dependent neuronal fluorescent signals failed to produce functional maps using the same procedures.
source: We verified the calcium specificity of STMs (reflecting underlying neuronal activity) by imaging Thy-1 GFP-M mice (n = 6 mice) that lacked calcium-dependent neuronal fluorescent signals and failed to produce functional maps using the same procedures (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is a control experiment verifying calcium specificity.

claim: Stable STM maps were generally observed using 256 spikes.
source: To investigate the sensitivity of the technique, the minimum number of spikes needed to make maps in GCaMP mice was measured by quantifying the similarities of pairs of STMs generated from a subset of increasing numbers of spikes. Stable STM maps were generally observed using 256 spikes (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is a finding about the minimum data requirements.

claim: A high stability of STMs was confirmed by comparing the maps generated by splitting a unit's spikes into two halves, or into odd and even groups which yield similar STMs.
source: A high stability of STMs was also confirmed by comparing the maps generated by splitting a unit's spikes into two halves, or into odd and even groups which yield similar STMs.
evidence: This describes a validation approach for STM stability.

claim: Electrode tracks were confirmed by labeling probes with Texas red-dextran or DiI to visualize tracks.
source: By combining wide-field calcium imaging and single unit recording, the mesoscopic network associated with any neuron of the brain can be mapped. After establishing the method, we then focused on thalamic and cortical recordings of spiking neurons and confirmed their anatomical location by labeling probes with Texas red-dextran or DiI to visualize tracks (Figure 3A, four experiments subcortical track and nucleus identification, see also Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This describes the anatomical verification method.

claim: Spiking cortical neurons were linked to consensus local and long-range cortical networks as defined by the stability of STMs between recordings.
source: We observed that spiking cortical neurons were linked to consensus local and long-range cortical networks as defined by the stability of STMs between recordings (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding about cortical neurons.

claim: Consensus cortical networks are those that can be identified by assessment of correlated activity (seed pixel analysis) and reflect major mono-synaptic intra-cortical axonal projections.
source: We define consensus cortical networks as those that can be identified by assessment of correlated activity (seed pixel analysis) and reflect major mono-synaptic intra-cortical axonal projections (Mohajerani et al., 2013).
evidence: This defines a key concept with citation.

claim: Spiking barrel cortex neurons were consistently linked to regional GCaMP signal changes in the barrel and motor cortex, as well as showing signals in homotopic areas of both hemispheres.
source: Spiking barrel cortex neurons were consistently linked to regional GCaMP signal changes in the barrel and motor cortex, as well as showing signals in homotopic areas of both hemispheres, consistent with the previously observed pattern of long-distance connections (Ferezou et al., 2007; Mohajerani et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2014; Vanni and Murphy, 2014; Chan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Cortical STMs computed from single unit activity or MUA strongly resembled one another and did not vary greatly according to laminar depth.
source: Cortical and thalamic STMs computed from single unit activity or MUA strongly resembled one another and did not vary greatly according to laminar depth.
evidence: This is a finding comparing different types of triggered maps.

claim: LFP-triggered STMs for delta band activity were similar to STMs.
source: LFP-triggered STMs for delta band activity were similar to STMs, while those associated with higher frequency bands showed more unique patterns that will be investigated in future work (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding about LFP-triggered maps.

claim: LFP-triggered STMs associated with higher frequency bands showed more unique patterns.
source: LFP-triggered STMs for delta band activity were similar to STMs, while those associated with higher frequency bands showed more unique patterns that will be investigated in future work (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding about higher frequency LFP bands.

claim: Delta band activity is where most mesoscale power functional imaging indicator power is located.
source: Delta band activity is where most mesoscale power functional imaging indicator power is located (Chan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: STMs for single thalamic neurons indicated a functional link between GCaMP maps and their consensus cortical projection areas.
source: STMs for single thalamic neurons indicated not only a functional link between GCaMP maps and their consensus cortical projection areas (Hunnicutt et al., 2014; Oh et al., 2014; Zingg et al., 2014) but also showed more variability and complexity in behavior than for cortical units.
evidence: This is a finding supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Thalamic neurons showed more variability and complexity in behavior than cortical units.
source: STMs for single thalamic neurons indicated not only a functional link between GCaMP maps and their consensus cortical projection areas (Hunnicutt et al., 2014; Oh et al., 2014; Zingg et al., 2014) but also showed more variability and complexity in behavior than for cortical units.
evidence: This is a primary finding comparing thalamic and cortical neurons.

claim: Thalamic neurons were associated with both unilateral and bilateral hemispheric signals within multiple primary sensorimotor and higher order brain areas.
source: Thalamic neurons were associated with both unilateral and bilateral hemispheric signals within multiple primary sensorimotor and higher order brain areas (Figure 3C).
evidence: This describes the spatial patterns of thalamic STMs.

claim: Cortical neurons in the same functional region exhibited substantial similarity in STMs.
source: To quantify the difference of variability of STM between cortical and thalamic units, we compared the percentage overlap of static STMs (Figure 3D; red areas) for neighboring pairs of neurons (100 μm apart). We found cortical neurons in the same functional region exhibited substantial similarity, while subcortical neurons had more diversity even within the same sub-nucleus in thalamus (i.e. VPL, VPM, see Table 1 for nomenclature and compare 3 example in Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about cortical neuron similarity.

claim: Subcortical neurons had more diversity in STMs even within the same sub-nucleus in thalamus.
source: We found cortical neurons in the same functional region exhibited substantial similarity, while subcortical neurons had more diversity even within the same sub-nucleus in thalamus (i.e. VPL, VPM, see Table 1 for nomenclature and compare 3 example in Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about thalamic neuron diversity.

claim: The contours of static STMs were largely similar between and within superficial and deep cortical layers.
source: The use of multichannel probes allowed us to obtain spiking profiles across cortical layers. However, there were only subtle topographic changes: the contours of static STMs were largely similar between and within superficial and deep layers, respectively (see the contour map in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding about laminar differences in cortical STMs.

claim: Sub-cortical derived maps were more varied than cortical maps when comparing STMs derived from neighboring electrode contacts.
source: To assess diversity in single neuron spiking derived cortical maps (STMs), we compared STMs derived from neighboring electrode contacts and found that sub-cortical derived maps were more varied (Figure 3Diii)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding comparing cortical and subcortical map diversity.

claim: Single cortical neuron-derived STMs were largely predicted by the pattern of cortical connectivity using SPM correlation mapping.
source: Single cortical neuron-derived STMs were largely predicted by the pattern of cortical connectivity using SPM correlation mapping (Figure 4A) as correlations were relatively high between these SPMs and STMs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding about the relationship between STMs and SPMs for cortical neurons.

claim: Thalamic STMs were more complex and corresponded to more unique distributions of cortical patterns and had significantly lower correlations with the cortical consensus SPM library.
source: In contrast, thalamic STMs were more complex and corresponded to more unique distributions of cortical patterns and had significantly lower correlations with the cortical consensus SPM library (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding comparing thalamic and cortical STMs to SPMs.

claim: It is possible that the cortical STMs derived from single spiking sub-cortical neurons are the super-position of 2 or more cortical networks defined by SPMs.
source: In other words, it is possible that the cortical STMs derived from single spiking sub-cortical neurons are the super-position of 2 or more cortical networks defined by SPMs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the nature of subcortical STMs.

claim: STMs of spiking cortical neurons correspond with underlying structural axonal projections.
source: As expected, we found that STMs of spiking cortical neurons correspond with underlying structural axonal projections (see BCS1 example in Figure 5, [Mohajerani et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is a finding comparing functional and structural connectivity with citation.

claim: Sub-cortical STMs cannot be predicted by direct monosynaptic projections from sub-cortical to cortical areas.
source: However, sub-cortical STMs cannot be predicted by direct monosynaptic projections from sub-cortical to cortical areas.
evidence: This is a finding about the relationship between subcortical STMs and anatomy.

claim: The HPF has no strong direct structural link to RS area.
source: For example, the HPF has no strong direct structural link to RS area.
evidence: This is an example supporting the claim about subcortical STMs and anatomy.

claim: CP was not directly linked to BCS1/HLS1 areas.
source: Furthermore, CP was not directly linked to BCS1/HLS1 areas (Hunnicutt et al., 2014; Oh et al., 2014), indicating that sub-cortical STMs reflect apparently polysynaptic links to cortex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Sub-cortical STMs reflect apparently polysynaptic links to cortex.
source: Furthermore, CP was not directly linked to BCS1/HLS1 areas (Hunnicutt et al., 2014; Oh et al., 2014), indicating that sub-cortical STMs reflect apparently polysynaptic links to cortex.
evidence: This is an inference from the anatomical comparison.

claim: The cortical calcium dynamics associated with spiking cortical neurons were relatively homogeneous with an initial peak in activity within ~100 ms – 200 ms following spiking and a return to baseline.
source: As observed for static STMs, the cortical calcium dynamics associated with spiking cortical neurons were relatively homogeneous with an initial peak in activity within ~100 ms – 200 ms following spiking and a return to baseline (Figure 6A).
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of cortical STMs.

claim: Some cortical cells (~20%) participated in multi-second depression dynamics.
source: However, some cortical cells (~20%) participated in multi-second depression dynamics (see distribution of profiles in Figures 7B,C and and 8A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about a subset of cortical cells.

claim: STMTDs generated by thalamic cells were more varied and were dominated by depression dynamics (~80% of cells) lasting up to 3 s.
source: In contrast, STMTDs generated by thalamic cells were more varied and were dominated by depression dynamics (~80% of cells) lasting up to 3 s (Figures 6B and 7B,C and Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about thalamic cell dynamics.

claim: Both STMs and STMTDs are similar across spiking modes to the all-spike average STMs in both cortical and thalamic cells examined.
source: We found that both STMs and STMTDs are similar across spiking modes to the all-spike average STMs in both cortical and thalamic cells examined (Figure 6—figure supplements 1, 2 and 3; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a finding about the robustness of STMs across different firing patterns.

claim: Manually partitioning the motifs into groups of four or more, and removing the spontaneous motif average, revealed that the sub-group STMs were the same as the overall average.
source: Manually partitioning the motifs into groups of four or more, and removing the spontaneous motif average, revealed that the sub-group STMs were the same as the overall average (Figure 6—figure supplements 4 and 5; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a finding about the stability of STMs across different groupings.

claim: The averaging method reveals how single cells participate in largely stereotyped networks despite the variability of ongoing cortical activity.
source: These tests confirm that the averaging method reveals how single cells participate in largely stereotyped networks despite the variability of ongoing cortical activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings about STM stability.

claim: Spike-triggered variance maps revealed similar brain regions as defined using spike-triggered average (STA) mapping when examined as a difference to baseline.
source: Spike-triggered variance maps revealed similar brain regions as defined using spike-triggered average (STA) mapping when examined as a difference to baseline (Figure 6—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a finding comparing variance and average mapping approaches.

claim: Using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) the time courses of STMTDs were clustered in three patterns.
source: Using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) we plotted the distribution of 428 STMTDs from both cortical and subcortical cells (Figure 7B). The time courses were then clustered in three patterns of STMTDs (using k-means algorithm) and averaged.
evidence: This describes the clustering analysis of temporal dynamics.

claim: The three STMTD patterns were termed: pattern #1: spike-triggered-excitation; pattern #2 spike-triggered inhibition; pattern #3 inhibition-triggered spiking followed by inhibition.
source: Based on their temporal relationship to spikes, we termed them: pattern #1: spike-triggered-excitation; pattern #2 spike-triggered inhibition; pattern #3 inhibition-triggered spiking followed by inhibition (Figure 7Ci).
evidence: This defines the three temporal patterns identified.

claim: ~80% cortical neurons were associated with a pure cortical excitation profile (pattern #1) and 20% triggered inhibition (pattern #2).
source: This classification showed that ~80% cortical neurons were associated with a pure cortical excitation profile (pattern #1) and 20% triggered inhibition (pattern #2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about cortical neuron temporal patterns.

claim: Only 20% of thalamic neurons associated with post-spiking cortical excitation, while 80% of were associated with cortical inhibition patterns (45% with pattern #2% and 35% with pattern #3).
source: In contrast, only 20% of thalamic neurons associated with post-spiking cortical excitation, while 80% of were associated with cortical inhibition patterns (45% with pattern #2% and 35% with pattern #3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about thalamic neuron temporal patterns.

claim: Pattern #3 was only identified with subcortical neuron spiking.
source: Notably, pattern #3 was only identified with subcortical neuron spiking.
evidence: This is a finding about the uniqueness of pattern #3 to subcortical neurons.

claim: Neither cortical cell depth, subcortical cell location, nor cell-type classification revealed any significant correlations between temporal dynamic clusters and cell-classification.
source: Neither cortical cell depth, subcortical cell location (e.g. VPM vs VPL), nor cell-type classification (inhibitory and excitatory types [Connors and Gutnick, 1990; Nowak et al., 2005]) revealed any significant correlations between temporal dynamic clusters and cell-classification (not shown).
evidence: This is a negative finding about correlations with cell properties.

claim: Aggregate cortical neuron spikes were generally followed by strong periods of persistent activation.
source: We found that as observed for individual neuron STMTDs, aggregate cortical neuron spikes were generally followed by strong periods of persistent activation (Figure 8A)
evidence: This is a finding about aggregate cortical neuron behavior.

claim: Sub-cortical neurons were linked to more diverse cortical activity profiles, in particular longer depression across multiple cortical ROIs.
source: whereas sub-cortical neurons were linked to more diverse cortical activity profiles, in particular longer depression across multiple cortical ROIs (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a finding about aggregate subcortical neuron behavior.

claim: STA generated from periods of quietness did not differ from those generated with all spikes.
source: STA generated from periods of quietness did not differ from those generated with all spikes (see Materials and methods, Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding about the impact of movement on STMs.

claim: Even when some movement could be observed during recordings, they minimally contribute to the mapping.
source: This suggests that, even when some movement could be observed during recordings, they minimally contribute to the mapping.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the movement analysis.

claim: Periods of high movement were relatively rare in awake head-fixed mice under the conditions employed.
source: This data also indicated that periods of high movement were relatively rare in awake head-fixed mice under the conditions we have employed and contributed negligibly to overall STA maps.
evidence: This is a finding about the behavioral state during recordings.

claim: Brain imaging activity obtained in awake states is mostly indicative of a quiet awake state and is not primarily movement-related activity.
source: Therefore, brain imaging activity obtained in awake states is mostly indicative of a quiet awake state and is not primarily movement-related activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral and imaging data.

claim: Increases in blood volume are expected to decrease both excitation and emission light.
source: Increases in blood volume are expected to decrease both excitation and emission light.
evidence: This is based on known optical properties of blood.

claim: The multi-wavelength corrections in practice did not appreciably alter cortical or thalamic STA maps or dynamics altering peak % ΔF/F0 by more than 1/10 of the maximum ΔF/F0.
source: While we have implemented a multi-wavelength correction strategy (see Materials and methods), the corrections in practice did not appreciably alter cortical or thalamic STA maps or dynamics altering peak % ΔF/F0 by more than 1/10 of the maximum ΔF/F0.
evidence: This is a finding about the impact of hemodynamic corrections.

claim: The short blue reference signal correlated positively with apparent blood volume artifacts that were revealed by parallel experiments using green reflected light imaging.
source: In these examples, we employ a short blue reference signal that correlated positively with apparent blood volume artifacts that were revealed by parallel experiments using green reflected light imaging (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This describes the validation of the hemodynamic correction strategy.

claim: The ratio of green over blue signal greatly reduced the blood volume hemodynamic response.
source: Consequently, the ratio of green over blue signal greatly reduced the blood volume hemodynamic response.
evidence: This describes the effectiveness of the correction strategy.

claim: Using GCaMP mice, where much larger activity-dependent signals were present, there was only a relatively small apparent contribution of blood volume to cortical and subcortical STA fluorescent signals.
source: Although the approach was effective at removing smaller non-specific signals in GFP-m mice, in practice, using GCaMP mice, where much larger activity-dependent signals were present, we revealed only a relatively small apparent contribution of blood volume to cortical and subcortical STA fluorescent signals as in other work (Vanni and Murphy, 2014; Murphy et al., 2016; Silasi et al., 2016) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This is a finding about hemodynamic contributions supported by citations.

claim: Thalamic STA maps and STA dynamic plots still indicated cases where thalamic spiking was associated with cortical inhibition after hemodynamic correction.
source: Furthermore, thalamic STA maps and STA dynamic plots still indicated cases where thalamic spiking was associated with cortical inhibition.
evidence: This confirms that the main findings persist after correction.

claim: STMs can reveal functional cortical architecture related to the activity of individual cortical and subcortical-cortical neurons.
source: Our results demonstrate that STMs can reveal functional cortical architecture related to the activity of individual cortical and subcortical-cortical neurons.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding.

claim: Cortically recorded STMs reflect the cortical state when a neuron spikes in connected areas.
source: Cortically recorded STMs reflect the cortical state when a neuron spikes in connected areas.
evidence: This is an interpretation of cortical STM findings.

claim: The STMs of individual sub-cortical neurons had more variation than maps attributed to spiking cortical neurons.
source: We observed that the STMs of individual sub-cortical neurons had more variation than maps attributed to spiking cortical neurons.
evidence: This is a primary comparative finding.

claim: Sub-cortical STM patterns of neighboring neurons were more diverse than cortical neurons.
source: For example, sub-cortical STM patterns of neighboring neurons were more diverse than cortical neurons, and were less likely to match intra-cortical consensus activity patterns defined using SPM.
evidence: This is a specific example of subcortical diversity.

claim: Sub-cortical-neuron-derived STMs revealed multiple areas of activation and multimodal kinetic behavior.
source: Sub-cortical-neuron-derived STMs revealed multiple areas of activation and multimodal kinetic behavior, while intra-cortical spiking neuron networks were simpler in structure and kinetics.
evidence: This is a comparative finding about complexity.

claim: Intra-cortical spiking neuron networks were simpler in structure and kinetics than sub-cortical networks.
source: Sub-cortical-neuron-derived STMs revealed multiple areas of activation and multimodal kinetic behavior, while intra-cortical spiking neuron networks were simpler in structure and kinetics.
evidence: This is a comparative finding about cortical networks.

claim: Spiking sub-cortical neurons reflected diverse cortical multi-phasic excitation/inhibition timing patterns that were reflected in dynamic STMTDs.
source: Furthermore, spiking sub-cortical neurons reflected diverse cortical multi-phasic excitation/inhibition timing patterns that were reflected in dynamic STMTDs.
evidence: This describes the temporal complexity of subcortical STMs.

claim: Most spiking cortical neurons were linked to a single phase of cortical excitation.
source: In contrast, most spiking cortical neurons were linked to a single phase of cortical excitation.
evidence: This describes the temporal simplicity of cortical STMs.

claim: The neocortex is divided into discrete subdivisions where individual spiking cortical neurons generally belong to spatial-temporal maps that follow a consensus function.
source: Our results indicate that the neocortex is divided into discrete subdivisions where individual spiking cortical neurons generally belong to spatial-temporal maps that follow a consensus function that can be defined using correlation as in previous work (Mohajerani et al., 2013; Chan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citations.

claim: Single thalamic neurons tend to fire when cortex is in more kinetically diverse states which is dominated by inhibition.
source: In contrast, we show that single thalamic neurons tend to fire when cortex is in more kinetically diverse states which is dominated by inhibition.
evidence: This is a primary finding about thalamic neuron behavior.

claim: The more diverse dynamics between thalamic neurons and cortical mesoscopic networks indicate that sub-cortical thalamic neurons play an instructive role with respect to cortical state, particularly with respect to feedforward cortical inhibition.
source: The more diverse dynamics between thalamic neurons and cortical mesoscopic networks indicate that sub-cortical thalamic neurons play an instructive role with respect to cortical state, particularly with respect to feedforward cortical inhibition (Stroh et al., 2013; Urbain et al., 2015)
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Cortical neurons may serve as relay endpoints or amplifiers.
source: whereas cortical neurons may serve as relay endpoints or amplifiers (Douglas et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about cortical neuron function with citation.

claim: The diversity in sub-cortical spiking derived maps may reflect differing receptive field properties in thalamus and cortex based on varying types of functional convergence.
source: The diversity in sub-cortical spiking derived maps may also reflect differing receptive field properties in thalamus and cortex based on varying types of functional convergence described previously (Miller et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the source of diversity with citation.

claim: In the somatosensory whisker barrel system, evidence for 'ensemble convergence' has been described where input from the thalamus can extend outside of the boundaries of the corresponding cortical receptive field.
source: Indeed, in the somatosensory whisker barrel system, evidence for 'ensemble convergence' has been described where input from the thalamus can extend outside of the boundaries of the corresponding cortical receptive field (Simons and Carvell, 1989; Linden and Schreiner, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The larger diversity of maps derived from the spiking of different thalamic neurons may be expected because of the smaller size of thalamic nuclei compared to the cortex and the recording of thalamic neurons from more-varied structures.
source: The larger diversity of maps derived from the spiking of different thalamic neurons may be expected because of the smaller size of thalamic nuclei compared to the cortex and the recording of thalamic neurons from more-varied structures.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the source of thalamic diversity.

claim: Thalamocortical impulses can be comprised of patterns of activity ranging from tonic, 'relay' transmission consisting of high regular rates of firing to burst-like activity where firing rates are low and interspersed with high-frequency events.
source: Another potential source of variance may arise from the diversity of thalamocortical impulses that can be comprised of patterns of activity ranging from tonic, 'relay' transmission consisting of high regular rates of firing to burst-like activity where firing rates are low and interspersed with high-frequency events (Steriade and Llinas, 1988; McCormick and Feeser, 1990; Sherman and Guillery, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Thalamic bursting can powerfully activate neocortical circuits and has been suggested to serve a 'wake-up' signal to sensory cortices.
source: Thalamic bursting can powerfully activate neocortical circuits and has been suggested to serve a 'wake-up' signal to sensory cortices (Sherman and Guillery, 1996; Swadlow and Gusev, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: When recordings were segregated into various firing configurations, no profound differences in STMs or their temporal dynamics were observed.
source: When we segregated our recordings into various firing configurations, we did not observe profound differences in STMs or their temporal dynamics indicating that the averaging methodology is not constrained by a particular firing pattern.
evidence: This is a finding about the robustness of the method.

claim: The averaging methodology is not constrained by a particular firing pattern.
source: When we segregated our recordings into various firing configurations, we did not observe profound differences in STMs or their temporal dynamics indicating that the averaging methodology is not constrained by a particular firing pattern.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the firing pattern analysis.

claim: STMTDs indicate slower time to peak (~100 ms) than postsynaptic potentials evoked by a single synaptic connection (time to peak ~20 ms).
source: Analysis of STMTDs indicate slower time to peak (~100 ms) than postsynaptic potentials evoked by a single synaptic connection (time to peak ~20 ms) (Bruno and Sakmann, 2006).
evidence: This is a finding about temporal dynamics with citation for comparison.

claim: Slower dynamics are expected given the kinetics of GCaMP6.
source: Slower dynamics are expected given the kinetics of GCaMP6 (Chen et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is an explanation based on known indicator properties with citation.

claim: Deconvolution resulted in a significant acceleration of raw data but very modest effects on STMTD.
source: We have used deconvolution (Pnevmatikakis et al., 2016) to take into consideration the slower kinetics of GCaMP6 and compensate for it. Using this approach, we observed a significant acceleration of raw data but very modest effects on STMTD
evidence: This is a finding about the effect of deconvolution.

claim: STMTD may already be accelerated relative to GCaMP6 kinetics by the statistical nature of spike/Ca2+ transient temporal convergence.
source: indicating that STMTD may already be accelerated relative to GCaMP6 kinetics by the statistical nature of spike/Ca2+ transient temporal convergence.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about why deconvolution has modest effects.

claim: Slower dynamics of STMTD may reflect sequences of spiking activity propagating through specific polysynaptic circuits.
source: It is also possible that slower dynamics of STMTD reflect sequences of spiking activity propagating through specific polysynaptic circuits.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis about STMTD dynamics.

claim: This speculation was supported by the similar time range of STMTD and cue-triggered recall of learned temporal sequences.
source: This speculation was supported by the similar time range of STMTD and cue-triggered recall of learned temporal sequences (Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This provides support for the hypothesis with citation.

claim: During specific behaviors we do not expect major shifts in area map boundaries found during spontaneous activity, as these are largely determined by projection anatomy.
source: During specific behaviors we do not expect major shifts in area map boundaries found during spontaneous activity, as we believe these are largely determined by projection anatomy (Mohajerani et al., 2013; O'Connor et al., 2013; Oh et al., 2014; Zingg et al., 2014)
evidence: This is a hypothesis about behavior-related changes with citations.

claim: During behavior we expect more nuanced changes in the weighting, timing, and frequency-dependence of STM networks during an active task.
source: During behavior we expect more nuanced changes in the weighting, timing, and frequency-dependence of STM networks during an active task.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about behavior-related changes.

claim: Thalamic neurons interact with cortex during specific state transitions that are not reflected by typical consensus cortical neuron behavior.
source: Our data have already revealed that thalamic neurons interact with cortex during specific state transitions that not reflected by typical consensus cortical neuron behavior.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding.

claim: The presence of obligate long-range relationships in even spontaneous activity may suggest new opportunities and routes by which brain stimulation and inhibition can be applied to affect synaptically connected areas.
source: The presence of such obligate long-range relationships in even spontaneous activity may suggest new opportunities and routes by which brain stimulation and inhibition can be applied to affect synaptically connected areas.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: Transgenic GCaMP6f mice were produced by crossing Emx1-cre, CaMK2-tTA and TITL-GCaMP6f strain.
source: Transgenic GCaMP6f mice (males, 2–4 months of age, weighing 20–30 g; n = 16), were produced by crossing Emx1-cre (B6.129S2-Emx1tm1(cre)Krj/J, Jax #005628), CaMK2-tTA (B6.Cg-Tg(Camk2a-tTA)1Mmay/DboJ, Jax #007004) and TITL-GCaMP6f (Ai93; B6;129S6-Igs7tm93.1(tetO-GCaMP6f)Hze/J, Jax #024103) strain (Madisen et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the mouse line generation with citation.

claim: These crossings are expected to produce a stable expression of calcium indicator variants specifically within all excitatory neurons across all layers of the cortex.
source: These crossings are expected to produce a stable expression of the three calcium indicator variants (GCaMP3, GCaMP6s and GCaMP6f [Chen et al., 2013b]) specifically within all excitatory neurons across all layers of the cortex (Vanni and Murphy, 2014).
evidence: This describes the expected expression pattern with citations.

claim: A 9 × 9 mm bilateral craniotomy covering multiple cortical areas was made.
source: A 9 × 9 mm bilateral craniotomy (bregma 3.5 to −5.5 mm, lateral −4.5 to 4.5 mm) covering multiple cortical areas was made as described previously (Mohajerani et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure with citation.

claim: Images of the cortical surface were recorded through a pair of front-to-front video lenses coupled to a CCD camera.
source: Images of the cortical surface were recorded through a pair of front-to-front video lenses (50 mm, 1.4 f:30 mm, 2 f) coupled to a 1M60 Pantera CCD camera (Dalsa) (Vanni and Murphy, 2014).
evidence: This describes the imaging setup with citation.

claim: Calcium indicators were excited with blue-light-emitting diodes with bandpass filters.
source: Calcium indicators were excited with blue-light-emitting diodes (Luxeon, 470 nm) with bandpass filters (467–499 nm).
evidence: This describes the excitation light source.

claim: Emission fluorescence was filtered using a 510–550 nm bandpass filter or collected in a multi-band mode.
source: Emission fluorescence was filtered using a 510–550 nm bandpass filter or collected in a multi-band mode as described below.
evidence: This describes the emission filtering.

claim: 12-bit images were collected at varying time resolution (20–100 ms; i.e., 10–50 Hz).
source: For single wavelength green epifluorescence, we collected 12-bit images at varying time resolution (20–100 ms; i.e., 10–50 Hz) using XCAP imaging software.
evidence: This describes the imaging parameters.

claim: Camera pixels were typically binned (8 × 8) producing a resolution of 68 µm/pixel.
source: In order to reduce file size and minimize the power of excitation light used, we typically bin camera pixels (8 × 8) thus producing a resolution of 68 µm/pixel.
evidence: This describes the spatial resolution.

claim: A multi-wavelength strategy was employed to correct for potential green epifluorescence signals associated with non-calcium dependent events.
source: In some experiments (as indicated), we employed a multi-wavelength strategy to correct for potential green epifluorescence signals that were associated with non-calcium dependent events.
evidence: This describes an additional correction method.

claim: The multi-wavelength strategy employed a variant of the spectral correction strategy that monitors changes in green reflected light near the isobestic point of hemoglobin.
source: We employed a variant of the elegant spectral correction strategy described by others (Ma et al., 2016; Wekselblatt et al., 2016) that monitor changes in green reflected light near the isobestic point of hemoglobin.
evidence: This describes the correction strategy with citations.

claim: Hemoglobin is assumed to be the primary absorber in brain tissue in vivo.
source: We assume hemoglobin is the primary absorber in brain tissue in vivo and changes in blood volume or oxygenation affect both excitation and emission of light used for wide-field imaging (Ma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an assumption with citation.

claim: Changes in blood volume or oxygenation affect both excitation and emission of light used for wide-field imaging.
source: We assume hemoglobin is the primary absorber in brain tissue in vivo and changes in blood volume or oxygenation affect both excitation and emission of light used for wide-field imaging (Ma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: This strategy provides a short blue light reference without the need for strobing which can limit time resolution and potentially entrain some neuronal rhythms.
source: This strategy provides a short blue light reference without the need for strobing which can limit time resolution and potentially entrain some neuronal rhythms (Iaccarino et al., 2016) and is more technically demanding from a hardware synchronization standpoint.
evidence: This describes advantages of the approach with citation.

claim: The short blue signal correlated positively (r = 0.93) with apparent blood volume artifacts revealed by parallel experiments using green reflected light imaging.
source: In preliminary analysis, we found that the short blue signal correlated positively with apparent blood volume artifacts that were revealed by parallel experiments using green reflected light imaging (r = 0.93, see Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding validating the correction method.

claim: Isoflurane and oxygen were stopped and the anesthesia mask was removed to initiate wakefulness.
source: To initiate wakefulness isoflurane and oxygen were stopped and the anesthesia mask was removed.
evidence: This describes the procedure for awake recordings.

claim: Calcium imaging data were obtained over 1 hr following cessation of anesthesia.
source: Calcium imaging data were obtained over the following 1 hr.
evidence: This describes the recording duration.

claim: Awake calcium imaging of spontaneous activity was performed in the absence of visual and auditory stimulation.
source: Awake calcium imaging of spontaneous activity was performed in the absence of visual and auditory stimulation.
evidence: This describes the recording conditions.

claim: A behavioral monitoring camera was used to confirm that the mice were indeed awake and relatively unstressed as grooming and whisking were occasionally observed.
source: A behavioral monitoring camera was used to confirm that the mice were indeed awake and relatively unstressed as grooming and whisking were occasionally observed.
evidence: This describes behavioral monitoring.

claim: An analgesic, buprenorphine, was injected 24 hr before awake calcium recordings.
source: An analgesic, buprenorphine, was injected (0.075 mg per kg body weight intraperitoneally) 24 hr before awake calcium recordings.
evidence: This describes the analgesic protocol.

claim: Raw extracellular traces were imported into Spike2 or SpikeSorter software for spike sorting and analysis.
source: Raw extracellular traces were imported into Spike2 (Cambridge Electronic Design, Cambridge, UK) or SpikeSorter software (Swindale and Spacek, 2014) for spike sorting and analysis.
evidence: This describes the spike sorting software with citation.

claim: Data were high pass-filtered at 1 kHz, and single spikes were detected using a threshold of 4.5 times the median of the standard deviation over 0.675.
source: Briefly, data were high pass-filtered at 1 kHz, and single spikes were detected using a threshold of 4.5 times the median of the standard deviation over 0.675.
evidence: This describes the spike detection parameters.

claim: Only units with a peak-to-peak extracellular amplitude of at least 40 μV, a minimum of 200 spikes, and a calcium cortical response of at least 0.5% were used for analysis.
source: For analysis, we only used only units with a peak-to-peak extracellular amplitude of at least 40 μV, a minimum of 200 spikes, and a calcium cortical response (STMTD, see next section) of at least 0.5% to improve single unit sorting isolation, STM map stability and signal-to-noise ratios for STMTD clustering (see main text), respectively.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for analysis.

claim: For each spike, the cortical fluorescence of every pixel during the period preceding the spike (−3 to 0 s: baseline) was averaged.
source: For each spike, we averaged the cortical fluorescence of every pixel during the period preceding the spike (−3 to 0 s: baseline).
evidence: This describes the baseline calculation method.

claim: ΔF/F0 was performed by subtracting and dividing the baseline to each frame for each spike within a time window of ±3 s.
source: ΔF/F0 was then performed by subtracting and dividing the baseline to each frame for each spike within a time window of ±3 s.
evidence: This describes the normalization method.

claim: STA sequences were created by averaging the ΔF/F0 responses for each trial and were compared with random spike STA.
source: STA (spike-triggered average) sequences were created by averaging the ΔF/F0 responses for each trial and were compared with random spike STA.
evidence: This describes the STA calculation method.

claim: STM temporal dynamics (STMTDs) were defined as the time course of activity of the maximally activated pixel in a region of interest.
source: STM temporal dynamics (STMTDs) were defined as the time course of activity of the maximally activated pixel in a region of interest.
evidence: This defines STMTD.

claim: The resulting clusters were separated using k-means clustering algorithm.
source: The resulting clusters were separated using k-means clustering algorithm.
evidence: This describes the clustering method.

claim: To calculate seed pixel correlation maps (SPM), the contribution of global and illumination fluctuations was subtracted from the signal of each pixel and the spontaneous activity recording sequences were temporally pass-band filtered (0.3–3 Hz).
source: To calculate seed pixel correlation maps (SPM), the contribution of global and illumination fluctuations was subtracted from the signal of each pixel (Vanni and Murphy, 2014) and the spontaneous activity recording sequences were temporally pass-band filtered (0.3–3 Hz).
evidence: This describes the SPM calculation method with citation.

claim: Cross-correlation coefficient r values between the temporal profiles of one selected pixel and all the others were calculated.
source: Then, cross-correlation coefficient r values between the temporal profiles of one selected pixel and all the others were calculated (White et al., 2011; Mohajerani et al., 2013; Vanni and Murphy, 2014).
evidence: This describes the correlation calculation with citations.

claim: Similarities between STM and SPM maps were performed by measuring the r-value Pearson correlation coefficient between each pair of pixels.
source: Similarities between STM and SPM maps were performed by measuring the r-value Pearson correlation coefficient between each pair of pixels.
evidence: This describes the map comparison method.

claim: Brain stacks of 140 slices were downloaded from the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas.
source: To compare the STM with anatomical database, brain stacks of 140 slices were downloaded from the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas providing AAV-virus tracing database (http://connectivity.brain-map.org/, [Oh et al., 2014]).
evidence: This describes the anatomical comparison method with citation.

claim: For each slice, the first dorsal 300 µm of brain fluorescence in the Z-axis were summed to generate partial maximum Z-projection maps.
source: For each slice, the first dorsal 300 µm of brain fluorescence in the Z-axis were summed to generate partial maximum Z-projection maps similarly to previous studies (Mohajerani et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the projection method with citation.

claim: Calcium imaging was temporally deconvolved pixel-by-pixel using the method presented by Pnevmatikakis et al. (2016).
source: We temporally deconvolved our calcium imaging pixel-by-pixel using the method presented by Pnevmatikakis et al. (2016) and code provided by the authors on Github (https://github.com/epnev/ca_source_extraction).
evidence: This describes the deconvolution method with citation.

claim: The method uses an autoregressive approach to estimate the calcium transient as an impulse response from the data itself.
source: Briefly, the method uses an autoregressive approach to estimate the calcium transient as an impulse response from the data itself (Pnevmatikakis et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the deconvolution approach with citation.

claim: The time course of calcium transients is deconvolved using a computationally efficient non-negative, sparse, constrained deconvolution.
source: Making use of this, the time course of calcium transients is then deconvolved using a computationally efficient non-negative, sparse, constrained deconvolution.
evidence: This describes the deconvolution algorithm.

claim: The method for defining main spiking modes requires determination of the distribution of each spike's inter-spike-interval (ISI) between the previous and following spike.
source: We implemented methodology previously described for defining main spiking modes (Sherman et al., 2006) (Figure 6.5, pg 236). Briefly, the method requires determination of the distribution of each spike's inter-spike-interval (ISI) between the previous (x-axis) and following (y-axis) spike (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the spiking mode analysis with citation.

claim: The vast majority of cortical cells recorded in barrel cortex did not exhibit multiple classes of spiking modes.
source: The vast majority of cortical cells we recorded in barrel cortex did not exhibit multiple classes of spiking modes (2 examples provided where some natural clustering is present: Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: This is a finding about cortical cell firing patterns.

claim: Only a few of thalamic cells recorded showed clear bursting modes while also passing minimum thresholds.
source: and only a few of thalamic cells we recorded showed clear bursting modes (two-examples provided Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D) while also passing our minimum thresholds (see Materials and methods: Single unit activity analysis).
evidence: This is a finding about thalamic cell firing patterns.

claim: Periods of quietness were identified as having a gradient lower than [median+σ/10], while periods of movement were higher than [median+σ].
source: Periods of quietness were identified as having a gradient lower than [median+σ/10], while periods of movement were higher than [median+σ].
evidence: This describes the movement detection criteria.

claim: An exclusion window of 10 s was applied at the beginning and the end of each period of quietness and only periods of more than 10 s were kept.
source: To more selectively identify periods of quietness isolated from any movement, an exclusion window of 10 s was applied at the beginning and the end of each period of quietness and only periods of more than 10 s were kept.
evidence: This describes the quietness period selection criteria.

claim: STA was generated only from spikes for periods of quietness and compared with STA of all spikes.
source: STA was then generated only from spikes for periods of quietness and compared with STA of all spikes.
evidence: This describes the movement control analysis.

claim: Data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism six and custom written software in MATLAB and Python2.7.
source: Data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism six and custom written software in MATLAB and Python2.7.
evidence: This describes the analysis software.

claim: Mann-Whitney non-parametric tests were used to compare correlation coefficients between STMs, percentage overlap between STM pairs, and the correlation coefficients between STMs and SPMs.
source: Mann-Whitney non-parametric tests were used to compare correlation coefficients between STMs, percentage overlap between STM pairs, and the correlation coefficients between STMs and SPMs.
evidence: This describes the statistical tests used.

claim: STMs included in analyses were generated from a minimum of 200 spikes.
source: STMs included in analyses were generated from a minimum of 200 spikes.
evidence: This describes an inclusion criterion.

claim: Only STMTDs exhibiting fluorescence exceeding 0.5% △F/F0 were used for analysis.
source: Only STMTDs exhibiting fluorescence exceeding 0.5% △F/F0 were used for analysis.
evidence: This describes an inclusion criterion.

claim: Sample sizes were not pre-determined but are consistent with previous experiments using similar methodology.
source: Sample sizes were not pre-determined but are consistent with previous experiments using similar methodology (Mohajerani et al., 2013; Vanni and Murphy, 2014; Chan et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the sample size determination with citations.
